speakeroldname: Hon. Robert Winters (Minister of Trade and Commerce):
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CERTAIN INITIAL PAYMENTS FOR NEXT CROP YEAR
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to inform the house of the government's decision on the level of the Canadian Wheat Board's initial payments to producers for the basic grades of wheat, oats and barley to be delivered during the 1967-68 crop year. The initial payments, effective August 1, 1967, will be as follows:
Wheat: No. 1 Manitoba northern, basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur or Vancouver, $1.70 per bushel.
Oats: No. 2 C.W. oats, basis in store Fort William/ Port Arthur, $0.65 per bushel.
Barley: No. 3 C.W. six row barley, basis in store Fort William/Port Arthur, $1.06 per bushel.
These payments represent an increase of 20 cents a bushel for wheat, 10 cents for barley and 5 cents for oats. The initial payments for all other grades of wheat, oats and barley will be established later by the Canadian Wheat Board.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Diefenbaker (Leader of ihe Opposition):
maintopic: ANNOUNCEMENT OF CERTAIN INITIAL PAYMENTS FOR NEXT CROP YEAR
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the initial payment is not the most important in determining what the farmer will receive. The extra amount announced is in keeping with the addition that was provided under the recent arrangements at Geneva. I repeat once more that as a consequence of this government's action in the last year and a half or two years in reducing the price by 17 cents a bushel, the western farmer will now be getting back that 17 cents plus a 3 cents addition.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES RESPECTING DISPOSITION OF EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there are a number of questions arising out of the critical and dangerous situation in the Middle East which I desire to address to the Prime Minister. Would he advise the house where the Canadian troops are now located, those who were members of the peace keeping force of the United Nations? What plans have been decided upon to evacuate them, and where will they be taken? Will they be sent tb another location in the Middle East rather than returned to Canada? Is it a fact, as reported in the press, that Canadian and United Nations troops have been deprived by the Egyptian forces of their transport and hospital facilities and supplies?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. L. B. Pearson (Prime Minister):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES RESPECTING DISPOSITION OF EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: The Canadian contingent of the United Nations force is in the Gaza strip. As far as details related to the other parts of the question are concerned, perhaps the Minister of National Defence would be in a better position to supply them than I am.

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Hellyer (Minister of National Defence):
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES RESPECTING DISPOSITION OF EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: The troops are in their camps operating normally and providing the services they are required to provide. The United Nations command has prepared a plan for the evacuation of the force, a phased plan which would see the forces of the various participating nations withdrawn over a period of several weeks. Due to the nature of the services provided by the Canadian contingent, the United Nations plans that our force will be one of the last, if not the last, to leave.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES RESPECTING DISPOSITION OF EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
Why?
Inquiries of the Ministry Mr. Hellyer: In addition to the United Nations plan the Department of National Defence has prepared a national contingency plan which can be put into effect if for any reason beyond our control or that of the United Nations the plan prepared by the United Nations becomes inoperable.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES RESPECTING DISPOSITION OF EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Why is it that the Canadians are to stay to the end? Why will they not be withdrawn in proportion to their numbers rather than kept in this dangerous position, providing a settlement is not arranged?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES RESPECTING DISPOSITION OF EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: There will be some phased withdrawal during that period; as the force can be diminished in size it will be done in the normal, routine way. I think the right hon. gentleman will appreciate that we provide support services for the UN force and that some of these services will be required during the period of evacuation.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES RESPECTING DISPOSITION OF EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: I have further questions on this subject, and I would ask the Prime Minister to reply to them. First, is it a fact-and I repeat the question-that Canadian troops are left without arms and without transport because of the action of the Egyptians?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES RESPECTING DISPOSITION OF EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: Does the Prime Minister say he has no information on that and has to wait for eventualities?

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES RESPECTING DISPOSITION OF EMERGENCY FORCE

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs, who in the last day or two has had discussions with the Secretary General of the United Nations, whether he can inform the house as to the reasons the Secretary General acted so precipitously in withdrawing the UNEF instead of seeking a meeting of the assembly or security council to discuss the matter?

May 23, 1967

speakeroldname: Hon. Paul Martin (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES RESPECTING DISPOSITION OF EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Secretary General, whom I saw on Saturday at the United Nations, informed me that he had ordered the withdrawal of the force for security reasons, and also because of the nature of the agreement concluded by his predecessor and President Nasser when the force was established in 1956.
I do not believe there is any difference of opinion between the secretariat and the position the Canadian government took, as I expressed it in the house on Thursday last, with regard to the authority required by the appropriate organ of the United Nations before the force loses its legal being within the terms of the resolution passed in 1956 when the force was set up.

subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES RESPECTING DISPOSITION OF EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext: I appreciate that the force may not lose its legal existence, but of what value is that legal existence if the force is withdrawn from the point at which it could be of assistance?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: MIDDLE EAST-INQUIRIES RESPECTING DISPOSITION OF EMERGENCY FORCE
speechtext:
Of course, Mr. Speaker, for all practical purposes my hon friend is right, but I simply dealt with the question in the terms of the position taken by the Canadian government in 1956 and in 1960. The United Arab Republic requested, as it had every right to request, the withdrawal of the force from its territory. In addition, two component countries of the force indicated that they did not propose to participate in the operations of the force in view of the position taken by the U.A.R. These additional reasons for the action taken by the Secretary General were announced by him at the meeting of contributing countries on Friday afternoon last.
Canada does not dispute the right of a host country to make a request for the withdrawal of a force. That request, however, is a matter that has to be considered by the responsible United Nations body in relation to the decision which the Secretary General took, and which he believed he had the authority to take.
I may say he has been queried as to what course he would take in the event of a request by another host country with respect to another United Nations force. Specifically, of course, Canada had in mind the case of Cyprus. To that the Secretary General replied that if such a request were made he would report it to the security council. He did not feel that in those circumstances he would be in any way inhibited, as he was in the case of

May 23, 1967

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I should like to ask the Minister of National Defence whether, inasmuch as the recent defence policy embodied in the unification bill was based largely upon the concept of Canada's defence forces in a peace keeping role, the minister is reviewing Canada's defence policy at this time in light of the undoubted setback to the concept of United Nations peace keeping forces, as a result of recent developments in the Middle East.

subtopic: REVIEW OF POLICY FOLLOWING CHANGE IN UN PEACE KEEPING ROLE

It is not my allegation; it is a statement carried by the press. The answer given by the Prime Minister is indicative of a
Foreign Policy
slapdash attitude on the part of this government respecting questions affecting the future of Canada and indeed the peace of the world.
The questions asked should have produced some information other than the type of circumlocution to which we have become accustomed in recent weeks.
I am amazed at the attitude of the government. Today I read according to the Canadian Press:
Cabinet Meets on Crisis
Prime Minister Pearson said "it's a tricky situation. I don't know how we're going to handle it."
This is not in keeping with the serious situation that prevails. It is strangely reminiscent of the type of answer given in the days when Mackenzie King was prime minister and he regarded external affairs as in his exclusive jurisdiction and indeed over and over again denied parliament information to which the house and country had a right.
I do not think it any exaggeration to say that at this moment the world is in fear. President Nasser demanded the removal of the United Nations peace keeping force. This force was mobilized from among seven nations. By its removal the Egyptian and Israeli armies will be facing one another. Egypt, Syria, Jordan, Iraq and Kuwait have mobilized; yet today the answers to unprovocative questions asked in the house were offhand as though they did not merit a serious answer.
U Thant was asked by President Nasser to order the removal of these forces. The government has taken two sides in this regard. The other day the Secretary of State for External Affairs announced in a loud voice that it was apparent that U Thant had acted precipitously; at least, so I interpreted his words.
I never said that at all.

A little later on it was confirmed by the minister that at the time the force was set up it was understood under arrangements between the then Secretary General and President Nasser that the force could not remain if his consent was withdrawn. U Thant has given outstanding leadership to the cause of peace. He is not in his position because he desired to remain aloof. At the end of his term last year, he was virtually conscripted to stay on because of his superior statesmanship. He had serious misgivings, to use his words, when he ordered the UN forces of Canada, India, Norway, Sweden, Denmark and Brazil to end their vigil on Friday last.

May 23, 1967
Foreign Policy
Today U Thant is in Egypt. What will be the consequences of the action taken the other day? Yesterday an announcement was made of the ban on shipping in the gulf of Aqaba. The U.A.R. has ordered total mobilization of its 100,000 man army reserve. Cairo's regular army within the precincts of Egypt numbers some 175,000 men. It has 40,000 still in Yemen. With the United Nations force emasculated as a result of the order, Egyptian troops now dominate the west bank of the gulf. The United States, Great Britain and France made a declaration in 1950 that they would "immediately take action, both within and outside the United Nations, to maintain the stability of all frontiers in the Middle East".
We meet in circumstances of dark and foreboding. Those who remember 1914 recall how suddenly war was with us. Canadians in that war made the supreme sacrifice of 60,000 men, greater than fell in the armed forces of the United States. I say that not by way of comparison but by way of emphasis on the danger that faces our nation and the world today. Before the second world war there were those events which ultimately culminated in war. What is going to be done now with the disbanding of the emergency force?
I do not understand the mumbo-jumbo language which the minister of defence uses -words large, sonorous and often meaningless. What is going to be done? One can get such words from Roget's Thesaurus. They give importance to announcements otherwise barren. Is there a plan in being which Canada can follow?
In my opinion, if the present emergency force goes out of existence it will be necessary to reconstitute it or another, otherwise the peace of the world will receive a setback from which it will not recover. Can a force be set up? The security council would have to bring the matter before its membership. It might be vetoed by the U.S.S.R. If the U.S.S.R. were to veto it, it would mean that country is determined, if war should break out, that it will not be an onlooker.
One of the major reasons for the terrible danger we now face in consequence of what is taking place in the Middle East is the direct fruit of the Viet Nam situation. In the Middle East Nasser has realized that the time is opportune for him to re-establish himself as the leader of the Arab countries. When I saw Nasser in 1964 he said "I have no intention of getting out of Yemen under any circumstances for three years". The Secretary of

State for External Affairs will recall that I so advised him then. The view of the department at that time was that Nasser had given his undertaking in the United Nations to remove his troops from Yemen within six months. His reply to me was that he had not undertaken to remove his troops; or at least if he had given the undertaking he had not undertaken as well not to substitute others for those moved.
[DOT] (3:20 p.m.)
The Yemen situation is a serious one. Aden brings to Great Britain problems almost beyond solution. Gibraltar is a danger spot. In Korea there are already divisions taking place and potential threats being made. In Hong Kong serious incidents are taking place. All over the world over a period of months there has developed a spirit of potential war. The same situation obtains in the field of trade but with that phase I do not intend to deal today.
Everywhere, Mr. Speaker, chaos threatens. We have asked the government over and over again for a debate so as to have before the house the views of the government. Nobody knows where the Canadian government stands on Viet Nam. Its ministers speak multilingually each advancing his own views regardless of the consequences to cabinet solidarity.
I am going to repeat what I said with regard to the views expressed by the President of the Privy Council, views diametrically opposed to the views expressed by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs. I have no doubt the hon. gentleman's mail is the heaviest ever received by any member of the House of Commons. Commendation for statements not in keeping with cabinet solidarity cannot be taken as an appropriate reward.
We have tried to get the government to agree to a debate. Various members-I have before me the excerpts from Hansard-have asked the government to set aside a couple of days for international affairs. The government has been afraid to permit discussion. It knows that uncertainty in its membership denies a declaration of unified policy.
In the last 48 hours the minister of manpower made a statement that what was said by the President of the Privy Council was not out of consonance with the views of the government. Each member believes he can make statements that will be attractive for the time
May 23, 1967

being, regardless of whether they are representative of government policy. Ministers go galloping off in many directions, each making statements which they regard as appropriate regardless of government policy.
This may not be the view of the government, Mr. Speaker, but it is the view of newspaper editorial writers in all parts of Canada. I wish to quote but one editorial in part from the Montreal Star for May 18 last, a newspaper never regarded as one of the warm hearted supporters of the Conservative view. The title is "Dangerous Habit Of Conning Electors", and it goes on to describe what has happened in connection with questions and answers about Viet Nam in this house. It says in part:
Instances could be multiplied. They are excused because of the belief in what has come to be known as "quiet diplomacy", by which is meant fixing something up before anybody can find out what is really going on.
That, Mr. Speaker, is representative of the view which is taken. The Halifax Chronicle-Herald has taken the stand that it was most proper to ask the government to bring before a committee of parliament the two journalists who made allegations regarding the international control commission. I do not think the government is very anxious to have them appear, because each of them has stated that such an opportunity would be welcomed, and the truth would then be forthcoming.
We are denied information. Information has become the privileged monopoly of the government. They seek to act on behalf of this nation without allowing parliament to find out what is going on. The only way to secure action is through the medium of an amendment. It will immediately be said that such an amendment, if supported, would constitute a vote of non-confidence. However, I would make the government an offer. We have tried in every way to get this government to give us an opportunity to find out what they are thinking about, if anything.
I will move this amendment, Mr. Speaker, but not for the purpose of prejudicing the government. If the government accepts the amendment it will in no way be considered by the opposition as a vote of non-confidence, but will constitute a declaration by parliament that this institution has the right to information. If the government falls in line with this suggestion I will make the immediate offer that if any subamendments are introduced by any third parties, those subamendments will not receive support from Her Majesty's loyal opposition. The purpose of
Foreign Policy
making this offer is to finally pry from this government information that is being denied to us.
What answers the Minister of National Defence gave hon. members in regard to the United Nations force and unification. The whole unification dream, now implemented into legislation, has disappeared in the last few days, as we in the opposition said it would. Today the minister is endeavouring to beat a strategic retreat.

Don't be irresponsible.
Perhaps it should not be called-
Don't be irresponsible.
-a strategic retreat.
Don't be irresponsible.

I will not argue. The minister beats what is being described as a strategic retreat, but I shall be glad to amend that and say that it is a disordered defeat. With the government's support he built up the idea of unification to create a mobile force, the objects of which were to reduce expenditure and to be available for peace keeping for the United Nations. The whole proposition was built on a quicksand of political illusion. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) rushed in to tell us that the creation of the unified force was in pursuance of our foreign policy and an adjunct thereto. Where is that policy today? It has all collapsed. One understands why the faces on the treasury benches are so long.
For weeks the government told us what a wonderful policy was being set up. They said that unification was not designed to turn Canadian forces into an international force. Again, may I be permitted to quote from the policy speech of the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) which he delivered two weeks ago. He said:
In circumstances such as these Canada, instead of stepping up her defence budget considerably, might decide to concentrate her efforts on the maintenance of mobile peace keeping or peace restoring units to be available to the United Nations on the shortest possible notice. This might make a lot of sense. Our new unified forces should be well suited to this task.

The creation of a mobile world peace keeping force as w'ell as elimination of waste are the goals of Canada's proposed reorganization of the armed

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Progressive Conservative Party House Leader
speechtext: General Allard's speech.
The government took the Canadian forces and dressed them up in little green uniforms. Now they are all dressed up with no place to go.
Oh, oh.

The peace keeping operation, as the minister admitted involuntarily in his answer a short time ago, will have to be looked into in the years that lie ahead. Those were his words earlier today, as I recall them.
The whole foreign policy of Canada, as a result of President Nasser's action reinforced by that of U Thant who could do nothing but what he did, has disappeared. All we have now is the unification legislation. "Royal" has gone. The basis for the legislation has ceased to exist. Is it any wonder that the faces of the government's ministers on Friday wore a look of defeat? They realized then for the first time that the unification legislation would create a force that would not defend Canada. We warned them the legislation makes the United States the defender of Canada and it provides forces for the United Nations to be used in all parts of the world whenever required.
Sir, this is a serious blow to policies not fully thought out and not reasoned out and what has happened completely supports the various high ranking officers who stated that the government's policy was a chimera, a dream. They said it would lower the morale of Canada's forces without bringing effective results. The government based its foreign policy on the assumption that what the UN had put together no man could put asunder. Today we face one of the most serious setbacks to international peace witnessed over the years.
I was in San Francisco in 1945 when the dream was for the creation of an international force to preserve and maintain the peace to be mobilized by the various nations comprising the United Nations. How this was to be done was not discussed. The great 
nations, with one exception, stood by the smaller nations, and the great nations had to assume the responsibility.
Sir, the first thing to be done is to restore an alternative force. Unless that is done the United Nations will be as powerless and impotent as was the League of Nations following the action in 1935 when Mussolini moved into Ethiopia. And what has happened now? The assembly is meeting. The charter gave the responsibility for peace keeping to the security council and, when the security council was not sitting, the general assembly by resolution could assume the authority for providing a United Nations force. The dreams of the charter have not been attained. The security council with the assistance of the military staff was to apply armed force for peace keeping. Today, whether it sits or not that committee has no authority. U Thant as secretary general has become the officer commanding the forces under the United Nations. The "unified for peace" resolution has not been acted on. At a time when the peace of the world is threatened what happens? The United Nations spent its time last week passing a resolution about West Africa and South Africa's mandate over it. It must have been realized that the resolution is almost unenforceable. Yet the problem facing the world has not been brought before the assembly. I hope that Canada acts at once to bring this matter before the assembly.
[DOT] (3:40 p.m.)
The war of nerves is on. We can only hope that as a result of what has taken place in the last few days there will be a realization of the terrible danger which faces the world. If the general assembly of the United Nations would meet now to deal with this matter and discuss it the danger might yet be averted. After all, it is a forum for discussion. Why has it not been empowered to deal with this matter? Why does it sit silent on everything except the West African mandate at a time when it should be dealing with a situation which threatens the peace of the world?
So far as the United Nations force is concerned, we asked earlier today what is to be done about the Canadian element. I cannot understand why the Canadian contingent should remain there the longest. We have been dedicated to peace keeping. We in Canada have been paying the cost of the United Nations force in Cyprus-without contribution and without thanks. Two weeks ago the U.S.S.R. indicated it would make no contribution to the cost of peace keeping.
May 23. 1967

The minister suggested the other day that the United Nations force now disbanded, to use his words, might be placed inside the Israeli boundary. If this were done we would be placing a non-United Nations force, a force unarmed except for small arms, in a dangerous position. It would be transformed ultimately into a combat force between Egypt and the other Arab nations, and Israel.
The situation of Israel is dangerous and threatening. I have seen the armed forces of that country through the inexperienced eyes of one who served in the lowest officer rank. There is wonderful morale in the Israeli forces. But they do not want war. It was never intended that the United Nations force should be used as a peace preserving unit. That means war. I asked the commanding officers of the United Nations force on two occasions how long they thought that force would last in the event of hostilities breaking out. The answer was: We would not last; we have no power; we are simply here in a supervisory capacity reporting on incidents which might ultimately lead to war. But we have no power or authority to act.
Furthermore, the ambassador for Israel said of the suggestion which was made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs that Israel receive a United Nations force on her territory:
There are legal difficulties there, because legally the force is no longer in existence.
I want to see Israel stand. I paraphrase the words of an English poet: Come what will, Israel yet shall stand. But to take a United Nations force and put it inside Israel within the territorial limits of that country would turn it into a combat force, unprepared as it is for combat.
I think the failure of the government to take a stand on the Viet Nam situation has been a major factor contributing to what is now happening in the Middle East. By this I do not mean that Canada is in any way responsible. The government has failed to take a stand on Viet Nam which could be understood. It has let Canada down before the world. One member of the administration backs the United States. Another says the United States has no moral right to be where it is. This creates a false sense of security in all parts of the world to the Canadian attitude. Indeed, the Washington Post of May 19 carried this headline following the admonition delivered by the Prime Minister extramurally at the conclusion of a recent cabinet meeting: "Canadian Cabinet Discord On
Foreign Policy
Viet Nam Papered Over". That is the response by a newspaper which has been friendly to Canada.
What about Viet Nam? I remember well the words of the Secretary of State for External Affairs when he spoke in this house on May 28, 1965, as reported at 1779 of Hansard. He said:
We know the North Vietnamese have taken advantage of social discontents to pose as the effective leaders of a reform movement. We know that by resorting to terrorism and blackmail they were able to establish control over large segments of the population and to organize the Viet Cong into an instrument of aggression directed, encouraged and supported on a grand scale since 1956 by men and equipment from the north. We believe there are at present over 35,000 highly trained guerrillas who have been infiltrated into the south from the north.
Further:
On the one hand we have the aggressive form of communism which sees wars that favour its purposes as "just wars". On the other we have the determination of the United States, for one. not to allow this aggression to be profitable, and the determination of the people of South Viet Nam to decide on their own future ...
Some people in this country-and if I interpret his comments correctly this includes the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam-appear to be advocating that the United States simply get out of Viet Nam. I wonder whether these people have really thought through what this would mean ...
If the United States withdraws from Viet Nam, how far is it to withdraw? Does it mean that Thailand, the Philippines and Malaysia, to mention only three of the nations most directly affected, are to be left to fend for themselves with nothing between them and an expansionist China? What about India, which has already had a bitter taste of China's expansionism? What is to happen to Australia and New Zealand?
In these words the Secretary of State for External Affairs took a stand. And he had the Canadian people behind him. Since then there has been all this tinkering by ministers, supported now by the Minister of Manpower and Immigration (Mr. Marchand) who is sympathetic to the views expressed by the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon). We say: Let it come to the peace table. That is the objective of all here. The attitude of communist China was revealed recently by Simon Malley who has just returned from Peking. He said:

China will send its vast armies into Viet Nam the moment Hanoi is threatened with a "sellout peace," Prime Minister Chou En-lai told me in his first interview with a foreign correspondent in two years.
He sat with me in his reception room in the Forbidden City of Peking and declared that Hanoi

has only to say the word to bring an avalanche oi Chinese "volunteers" to its aid.
Ultimately, he predicted, the course of events will result in just that.
Day after day over the C.B.C. we have a continual chorus being placed before the Canadian people that after all communism is not so bad. They advocate the United States get out regardless of the consequences. That proposition is a complete denial of the prospects that mankind faces.
This government has tried to be on both sides of the question of Viet Nam. At Temple University in Philadelphia the Prime Minister two years ago said:
No nation-and particularly no newly independent nation-could ever feel secure if capitulation in Viet Nam led to the sanctification of aggression through subversion and spurious wars of national liberation.
Today with the situation dark and difficult the government of Canada is on both sides of the Viet Nam question. It is at the same time on neither side. The ministers speak multilingually on foreign affairs regardless of the fact that in so doing they are failing to give leadership. I think, and I have never detoured from this position that the United States ought to carry out the appeal that was made by the United Nations Secretary General for a halt in the American air bombardment of North Viet Nam. I realize such a step would cause dangers and there are imponderables in the equation. There is no positive guarantee that it would bring about peace talks. It might enable the north to increase the flow of goods to the south and strengthen defences at home. All of this is true but, sir, let it be tried.
U Thant has said that he is afraid we are witnessing today the initial phase of world war III. No one knows what, if anything, will bring Viet Nam to the peace table but it will not be the mass evacuation of United States forces, a proposition which received such approval from the communist party in our country the other day in a release from communist headquarters. On the other hand, realizing the position of the United States I believe that there should be a bombing halt with a strenuous peace offensive by leaders everywhere in the western world.
Certainly what is happening today is frightening in its implications. Those of us who are older will not be there if war comes but the young men and women of this nation and of all the western nations will not stand idle. The other day five United States senators, both Republican and Democratic, came

out in favour of action along this line. The Democratic leader in the U.S. senate pleaded for such action. I would like to see our parliament, while realizing the tremendous contribution of the United States, make clear the view that such a bombing halt is necessary today. There will be no second prizes in the next world war.
Can we not hope that instead of being answered, as we were today, in a condescending manner, the government will come clean, will tell Canadians the facts, will let us know what the course is to be-not the unimaginative nonsense of the Minister of National Defence in setting up his personal plaything, the unified force. Let us have a declaration from the government of Canada as to what it intends to do and the course it intends to follow, denuded of these massive phrases and expostulations to which we are subjected from time to time. Let us have a statement in clear and unequivocal language.
It is on that basis that I move the amendment, and I repeat what I said when I began. There was no other course open to obtain from this government its views and the attitude of the administration. We tried to have by agreement discussion for a day or two on these matters. That was refused. We tried to bring about the convening of the foreign affairs committee, to bring before it those two Canadians, one of whom on the C.B.C. and the other in the Montreal Star, who by what they stated, if it is true, delivered up to all the world Canada's reputation for fairness and justice.
The criticism by these two men, who bear good reputations, deprived Canada of being in a neutral position on the International Control Commission. These two men should be given the opportunity to tell their story. If what they said is not true it should be so branded, but if it is true it is the utmost condemnation of this government. It shows that this government has been playing at walking down the centre of the street and pretending to do business on both sides of the street.
Therefore I move, seconded by the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Starr):
That all the words after "that" be deleted and the following substituted therefor:
"This house regrets that, despite repeated requests by honourable members, the government has neglected or refused to make available time to debate international problems which are so serious and dangerous that they could lead to world war III and further regrets that the government has failed to state the policies of our country with clarity, without uncertainty and unequivocally with regard
May 23, 1967

to Asia and the Middle East so that Canadians and freedom-loving nations will know where Canada stands.

Hear, hear.

speechtext:
I discussed with him the possibility that the United Nations truce supervision organization might be reactivated in Gaza and the Sinai as an aid to peaceful conditions in the area. He will look into the possibility and, I am sure, investigate what might be feasible in the light of the position of the government of the United Arab Republic in requesting the withdrawal of the United Nations emergency force. The Secretary General explained to me in detail his reasons, some of which I have given today in an answer to a question, for the step he took in answer to the demand, addressed in the first instance by the foreign minister of the U.A.R. to the general commanding the United Nations force. He circulated a report summarizing his position in that regard to the security council on May 19 last.
I told the Secretary General that I understood and respected his position even though we differed on certain aspects of the procedures involved, but that our only concern now in view of the decision he has taken is to be of whatever assistance we can to enable the United Nations to play a useful role in the area. This will depend in part on the results of his conversations in Cairo. I did express [Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1
the hope that he might find it possible to visit other countries in the region so that when he returned to New York he could give a complete report on steps that might be taken by the United Nations to ease the position and restore peaceful conditions.
I reminded him that in a similar situation in 1958, after the landing of marines in Lebanon and British forces in Amman and Jordan, the then Secretary General announced that he was going to see the president of the United Arab Republic, and it was while he was in Cairo that he indicated his intention, in the interests of establishing an equilibrium in the area, to visit Israel and Jordan, and indeed he went to Iraq.
It is my hope that the discussions the Secretary General will have in Cairo will make it possible for this balancing kind of visit to take place. I also spoke when I was in New York on Saturday to the ambassadors of the United Kingdom, France, the United Arab Republic, Israel and Syria. I would have welcomed as well an opportunity to speak to the ambassador of the Soviet union but he was not available.
I took the opportunity to explain to these spokesmen for their governments the views of the Canadian government and as well to obtain their views. I expressed our concern over the potentially dangerous situation which had arisen and endorsed the Secretary General's plea for restraint by all concerned. I made it clear to the representatives of governments from the area that Canada had no intention of abandoning its impartial attitude toward the problems of the Middle East and that our chief interest was to work out with the United Nations some solution to restore stable conditions in the area.
I also indicated that as a major contributor to peace keeping operations we were naturally anxious that nothing be said or done which would destroy the confidence that member states must have in the United Nations as a conciliator and impartial presence. Let me say that notwithstanding the present ineffectiveness of the United Nations in many areas this government believes in its potential strength and in its necessity as an institution in this interdependent nuclear world of ours.
While in New York I also discussed the role of the security council in the present situation. My right hon. friend spoke of the authority of the assembly. It must not be forgotten that the security council is the agency under the charter constitutionally set up to deal with situations that threaten the peace.
May 23, 1967



As we know, this does not preclude the general assembly, through the uniting for peace resolution, from asserting its view, but in so far as enforcement action is concerned this can only come, as I know my right hon. friend will recall, under the authority of the security council.
I indicated that the council ought to be in continuous session, with its members constantly available so as to be ready to act whenever necessary. I well recognize that there might be some danger of precipitating a premature confrontation in the council if it were to meet before the parties to the dispute were ready to agree to some interim steps which might be taken, perhaps as a result of the visit of the Secretary General. Naturally, if there were serious incidents or other developments which might lead the council members to believe there might be conflict, then the council could meet at once to deal with the situation. Yesterday's announcement by the president of the United Arab Republic that he was stopping Israeli shipping in the Gulf of Aqaba may require the council to meet.
Urgent consultation between the members is now taking place and Canada as a member of the council is participating in these discussions. There are considerations, as I am sure the house will realize, which must be very much in the minds of the members of the council before they decide to take particular steps or before they decide to meet.
President Nasser is reported to have stated in his speech last night that U.A.R. forces had occupied Sharm-el-Sheikh and that the U.A.R. would not permit a ship flying the Israeli flag to pass through the Gulf of Aqaba.

May I ask the Secretary of State for External Affairs whether President Nasser did not say more than that? Did he not also say he would not permit any ship carrying strategic material to enter the gulf?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That is right. He said he would not allow ammunition or materials of war to pass through.
I was just about to observe that this was one of the matters that the Secretary General will undoubtedly be discussing. I asked our representative on the council to take full part in the discussions in New York that are now taking place, and to note particularly the discussions that have already taken place between certain of the permanent members of the council.

The fact that the U.A.R. has asked for the withdrawal of the force and that two of the contributing members indicated they would no longer serve in the force-
Which two are they?

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
As I indicated last Friday in answer to a question by my right hon. friend, the two which took that position were India and Yugoslavia. These are considerations that have to be borne in mind in assessing the effectiveness of the force as an instrument of pacification. I welcomed this discussion in light of our experience in this particular kind of situation, but the difficult ties of maintaining a force must be borne in mind.
The United Nations truce supervision organization, essentially an observer group now with 120 men although at one time it had a personnel of some 700, has certain powers under the mixed armistice commissions created by the security council. These powers could enable it, together with certain other powers, to act as an effective international presence and a United Nations body to keep the peace between the conflicting parties. It may be that at this moment the time is not appropriate for putting this into effect, notwithstanding the desirability, because it must be remembered that such a force cannot be established without the consent of the parties involved, the host countries, in this case the United Arab Republic and Israel, nor can it be accepted in terms of an enlargement of powers by the security council unless all five of the great powers consent. So it will be understood why there should be consultations and negotiations prior to a formal meeting of the council.

I was not suggesting that there was any reason. I was simply told through our ambassador that it was not possible because of other arrangements that I presume the ambassador had made. The request came late, as indeed it did to all those I have seen. It was only late Friday that it was agreed I should go to New York. I do not believe there is anything more I can say about this situation. We all recognize how serious it is, particularly the sensitivity in the Gulf of Aqaba. Mr. Speaker, would the minister permit a very brief question at this point? speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
My understanding is that two ships have already gone through. I might mention in passing that the United Nations convention of April 29, 1958, on the territorial seas and contiguous zones provides for the right of innocent passage. This treaty has been signed and ratified by 33 countries. It has not been signed or ratified by Saudi Arabia or by the United Arab Republic. It was signed by Canada. It was not ratified by Canada for reasons, as my right hon. friend will know, that had to do with our negotiations regarding problems involving the law of the sea. But there is no doubt in my mind that this convention is declaratory of international law, which provides for innocent passage in respect of international waterways.
My right hon. friend came back, as he had every right and indeed as he has a duty to do, to discuss the problem of Viet Nam. This question has been the subject of persistent interrogation, and rightly so, in this house now for two and a half years. I would simply remind the house, and I do this not by way of

defence of any kind of response that I make to questions, that in all the parliaments which I have studied questions on international affairs are put following written notice. I have not taken refuge-
That is what the rules say, but you have not followed that course yourself.

-in this perfectly legitimate response that I could make, because I felt that we were entitled in this house to the fullest explanation wh.ch a minister in my circumstances and having my responsibilities could give. I think the record of this house and the record of the external affairs committee will show that the government's policy has been stated over and over aga.n in the only way in which it can be stated having in mind the nature of our role on the commission, the nature of diplomacy itself. In the interests of achieving what one hopes one m ght achieve as a result of the contacts which the government has in respect of a matter so delicate and important as the war in Asia, I hope this will be understood.
But I should like to repeat again that Canada is not a belligerent in this war. Canada did not start this war. On the government benches we have said that it is not the intention of this government to commit troops to that war. I have said in answer to questions that our commitment in that regard could only arise pursuant to an obligation inherent in the charter of the United Nations. That continues to be our policy. Because it has been said that in the long run more is to be gained by quiet diplomacy, the government has been charged, as my right hon. friend charged today, with refusing to give this house and the country information which it was entitled to have. I know my right hon. friend too well, however, to take all of his observations with the same serious intent that he would have me bestow on those observations. I have sat in this house with my right hon. friend a long time. I know his technique just as well as I am sure-
We know yours.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: -he has admiringly watched my technique.
Hear, hear.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
I saw a report the other day that my right hon. friend said how dangerous a thing was quiet diplomacy. One could almost imagine him conjuring up
May 23, 1967

Wilson and complaining about secret diplomacy as though quiet diplomacy and secret diplomacy were the same kind of thing or even the other side of the same coin. The real fact is that no one can carry on diplomacy unless it be quiet. It ceases to be diplomacy if it is not quiet. You would not be able-
You should tell Mr. Gordon that.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
-to enjoy the confidence of others if this were not the case. For instance, in my talks with the Secretary General I am sure that if I had not established a standard of credibility with him it would not have been possible for me to receive at his hands certain information which I believe to be very important and which I passed on to my colleagues in the government, as he has passed it on to certain other spokesmen for other governments.
It must also be understood that quiet diplomacy is not part of foreign policy, as some hon. gentlemen in this house, at least by implication, suggest. Quiet diplomacy is not policy. Quiet diplomacy is not a program. It is an instrument. It is a technique, and no one employed it, and rightly so, more successfully than my right hon. friend in certain situations such as that which confronted his government with respect to the Congo.
[DOT] (4:30 p.m.)
There are occasions when a government should not hesitate to make a public declaration of policy, but that is not inconsistent with the necessity, for instance, of Canada as a member of the commission treating matters with colleague states in a confidential way. Certainly that is the only way one would carry on discussions in this matter with the government of Hanoi, either through Mr. Ronning or through our present representative on the commission. Certainly one could not enjoy very long the confidence of any government unless one had created a reputation for respecting confidences and had won, as a result, a credibility where it is necessary for the Canadian government and other governments to make contacts if they are going to make their contribution to try to bring about an end to this very difficult and regrettable war in Viet Nam.
On this subject I would simply remind the house what a former Canadian diplomat, Mr. Escott Reid, pointed out the other day, namely, that quiet diplomacy is the application of sound practice in our relations with other countries. I hope that no one is going to say
Foreign Policy
the government is refusing to give information because it observes something that every government, in the conduct of its affairs with other countries, must do in the interests of satisfactory relations and the attainment of its objectives.
We are a member of the commission. We have been there for 13 years along with India and Poland. Charges of spying against our personnel are unfounded, and I regret that my right hon. friend brought that question up today. I want to say, as Secretary of State for External Affairs, that we have every reason to be proud of the soldiers who from 1955 on have served Canada on the commission. Certainly I as Secretary of State for External Affairs am proud of the record of integrity and purpose of the foreign service officers of the Department of External Affairs who under difficult circumstances have served the cause of peace and international conciliation in a way that should win expressions of gratitude and occasion the pride which I feel in this service and in what they have done as members of this commission.
When a year ago last January the Secretary General and I discussed the question of Viet Nam I was persuaded by his argument that the settlement of this problem must be within the framework of the Geneva conference. Regrettable as it was, the United Nations, the security council or the assembly, could not be expected to deal effectively with this problem because of the absence from its membership of particular countries involved. From that moment on we sought, as I have reminded the house time and time again, to impress upon India and Poland the desirability of constituting the three members on the commission into a body that might have as its prime purpose the narrowing of the gap between the parties, based on the fact that this instrument has a readier access to Hanoi and to Saigon than any other instrument. We have not been able to persuade all the members of the commission of the importance of this proposition although both Poland and India have recognized the potential role for the commission in this situation.
We did not limit our efforts only to our role as a member of the commission, but on two occasions we sent Mr. Chester Ronning as a special emissary of the government of Canada to Hanoi, to Saigon and to Washington for the purpose of seeing whether or not he, in the name of the government of Canada, could

May 23, 1967
Foreign Policy
make any progress in delineating the distances between the parties and seeing whether or not a formula could be reached which might at least bring about preliminary discussions between the parties involved in this war. I may say that on his first visit Mr. Ronning did bring back information which I believe was important, information which has since been partially made public but which I think, while not furthering the ultimate cause which he and the government had in mind, nevertheless has assisted us to understand the difficulties and perhaps the reasons for the inflexible position which both parties seemingly have taken in their declared positions.
Let no one say that the commission or the Canadian government has not been engaged ip trying to bring about peace. The record is there to judge when the time comes for its full exposure, and I venture to suggest that Canadians will not be ashamed of our efforts through this instrument to try to bring about peace in this situation.
We did not stop with these endeavours only. I went to the Soviet union and to Warsaw last November in connection with the war in Viet Nam. If I am not able to disclose fully the nature of the conversations which I had, it is not because these were not directed toward the kind of objective that we had in mind in the commission or toward the kind of objective that we have in mind now. Right from the beginning our position with regard to the war in Viet Nam has been that We wanted a cease fire. Right from the beginning we firmly declared our view that a military solution alone to this problem was neither desirable nor practicable. When a year and a half ago the unaligned nations made an appeal, Canada was the first country to join in that appeal. It will be recalled that we urged the United States to accept certain positions with regard to the 17-point appeal made by the unaligned nations.
My hon. friend says he is concerned about the war in Viet Nam. Is there anyone in this house who is not concerned about the war in Viet Nam? Is there anyone in Britain, in France, in Belgium, in the Scandinavian countries or in the United States who is not concerned? Governments which have particular information on certain aspects of this problem are not on that account excused from being concerned about the war in Viet Nam, about its escalation and expansion, about the dangers of further escalation and the dangers of involving other countries and of creating situations that could add to the intensity of the present conflict.
[Mr. Martin (Essex East).l
I am not asking for any sympathy from this house. I have been here too long to know the unwisdom of that kind of tactic. But I will say that the house has the right to know that as a member of this government charged with this matter there has not been anything that has occupied my time more or that of the Department of External Affairs than trying to achieve some success in the areas about which I have been talking in the past few minutes, and this has been shared by my colleagues in the government. No man has been more devoted to the cause of peace in his lifetime than the Prime Minister and it is only to be expected that any government of which he is the head would, as would a government headed by any other hon. member in the house including my right hon. friend, be anxious to bring about peace. We do not help to bring about that kind of condition when we charge, knowing full well that the government cannot take any other course, that the government is unwilling to give parliament and the public information, and when any hon. member who makes that charge knows perfectly well, if he knows anything about the conduct of foreign policy, that for the government to take any other course than the one it has followed would be irresponsible and would not be calculated to bring about peace.

Yes, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian government is concerned about the course of events in Viet Nam.
