speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
speechtext:
Order. Perhaps before the hon. member for Okanagan-Revelstoke (Mr. Johnston) continues his remarks he might let me read the subamendment which was moved by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis). First of all, I want to thank the members of the house for giving me the opportunity of considering this subamendment over the dinner hour.
The subamendment reads as follows. It was moved by the hon. member for York South, seconded by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles);
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end thereof to a comma, and by adding immediately thereafter the following words:
"and in particular this house regrets that the government has failed to do everything in its power to press the United States to stop the bombing of North Viet Nam, as a necessary preliminary to negotiations to end the war in Viet Nam".
The Chair has had an opportunity, as I said before, to consider the subamendment. While there are some reservations in the mind of the Chair, perhaps they are not particularly serious, and in view of the debate which is now taking place the Chair has decided to accept the subamendment.

Mr. Speaker, my concluding remarks will be very brief indeed. Wonder and surprise has been expressed in this debate that the Secretary General of the United Nations should have withdrawn the United Naitons peace keeping force so swiftly on application to do so from the United Arab Republic. But this does follow fairly logically. If the United Arab Republic only a few weeks ago was above criticism by the United Nations, or a committee of the United Nations, then it would follow that their wishes would be respected immediately by that organization when they came to demand that the peace keeping force be withdrawn.
I would suggest that the time has come for the United Nations, indeed all nations that are interested in maintaining peace in the world, to speak out. In addition, no nation, whether it be the United Arab Republic or any of the Arab states, a communist nation or indeed the United States itself, can be above criticism in today's world.

Mr. Speaker, I think there is one thing on which all of us in
May 23, 1967

this house are agreed, and that is that we are very much concerned about the numerous threats to world peace that are appearing in various areas of the globe. I also think we are all agreed that we in this house would like to see these threats removed by peaceful negotiation and settlement. Where we differ perhaps in some degree is in the best means of attaining this end.
I think it is quite safe to say that Canadians generally are very disturbed about these threats to peace which are being made throughout the world-in Viet Nam, in the Middle East, in Hong Kong and other places. People are disturbed because there is uncertainty, and there is nothing that disturbs people more in this world than uncertainty. People in Canada are disturbed about the objectives in Viet Nam of our closest friend and ally, the United States. People are very worried indeed about this. There is also uncertainty about what is intended by the Chinese in Hong Kong. We are uncertain as to what is intended by President Nasser in the Middle East.
Unfortunately, Mr. Speaker, I think these uncertainties are to some degree caused by the position taken by the government. As suggested in the amendment moved by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), the government has not explained its position. It has not forcefully stated the reasons for its policy or, indeed, what the policy is.
[DOT] (8:10 p.m.)
The government's difficulties in this regard have been compounded by parliamentary agencies such as the C.B.C. The right hon. Leader of the Opposition has noted that that organization has been running a steady propaganda campaign against the United States for a good many years and has been distorting the views and objectives of that country. Why they do this I do not know, but that has been going on. The general impression created in this country is that the people in the United States are like demons, and that they can do nothing right under any circumstances. Never a word is mentioned when the North Vietnamese or the Viet Cong place bombs in restaurants where there are women and children; that is perfectly all right. The result has been that the public of Canada has been misled considerably by this parliamentary agency, and that has caused much trouble.
Again, had the government been more ready with information about the reasons for the position of the United States and the
Foreign Policy
positions of others in Viet Nam, and if to counter adverse propaganda it had been more forceful in expressing reasons for its policy, it would not have to sit on the fence, so to speak and pussyfoot about its position.
There is something else I wish to mention before getting to the meat of my remarks, and that has to do with information. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) was vehement in objecting to observations from opposition members that the government had not been forthcoming with information about Viet Nam and other aspects of our foreign policy. His position was that the government has given out all the information it could give out. Of course this is all a matter of opinion; the minister had to decide to what degree information must be classified, and how much can be given out. I know that perfectly well. Yet last week, when noted members of the United States Senate and Congress were here at the annual meeting of the Canada-United States parliamentary group-there were such distinguished men as Senator Mansfield, Senator Aiken, Representative Gallagher, and Doctor Morgan who is Chairman of the house committee on armed services-we obtained more information from them on Viet Nam and China in two or three hours than we had been able to obtain here in the last couple of years. Those, men of course, may be in a better position to assess the importance of information than is our minister. I understand the minister's position; nevertheless the information we obtained was readily forthcoming and was very helpful.
The first of the two major problems concerning people in this country, as was suggested this afternoon by the right hon. Leader of the Opposition, is the Middle East. Perhaps the present situation, where the President of the United Arab Republic is pressing his demands on Israel, has flared up, or been prompted, because the United States is somewhat tied up in Viet Nam. President Nasser may have thought that this was the appropriate moment to press his demands. Also I cannot help feeling that the president of the U.A.R. may have been influenced by the presence of a certain gentleman who is well known to some members of this house and who is now active in Middle East and Near East politics-Doctor Shukari. He was for a long time at the United Nations, and he is a very dangerous and influential man. Knowing something of his character I have a feeling that he may have had some hand in

May 23. 1967
Foreign Policy
what is happening in the Near East; however, that remains to be seen.
The situation in the Near East is hard to analyse. It seems strange, that, had President Nasser really meant to attack Israel, he would not have gone to war without talking about it so much. Surely he would have invaded Israel and said nothing, had he really meant war, because in these days if you want to go to war, you surprise the enemy. Because there has been much sabre rattling during the last two or three days, gives credence to the belief that President Nasser is working at some sort of negotiating lever. On the other hand his threats may be genuine. Only time will tell.
I can suggest one thing to the minister: Canada is held in a great deal of respect in the United Arab Republic. It is safe to say that Canada is very highly thought of in that part of the world. I know that from experience, having dealt with the U.A.R., and I am sure that the minister has found the same thing.
I remember a little incident that took place a few years ago when Arab students were studying in the Soviet union. President Nasser found that they were receiving more propaganda than technical training, and withdrew them from that country. Canada offered to take these students, thus making a contribution to the United Arab Republic. I could mention numerous other incidents, at the United Nations and elsewhere, to illustrate my point.
In view of the esteem in which Canada is held in the U.A.R.-and we are almost equally well received in Israel-I suggest that Canada might quietly offer the good offices and services of some prominent Canadian, perhaps that might be the minister himself, to try to bring about some settlement in the dispute. I do not know whether that would be successful, but as the minister suggested, Canada should try to do these things. Over the years Canada has taken a leading part in activities such as this, and I think we should attempt something of that sort now. If our efforts do not succeed, nobody will be the loser. Yet there is a reasonable chance that by offering to use our good offices in this situation our offer might be accepted. In any event, I think we should try.
The right hon. Leader of the Opposition spoke at some length about the apparent folly of the government's policy of unifying the armed forces. Many of us sitting on this side warned the government during the debate of the great danger of putting all our eggs in one 
basket. We said that our forces should not be designed purely for United Nations peace keeping roles. We hope that the United Nations will recover from this present setback, and that it W'U increase its peace keeping activities in the future; yet the situation demonstrates, as the right hon. Leader of the Opposition said, how unwise the government was in unifying the armed services and in designing them for the undoubted purpose of being useful only as United Nations peace keeping forces. I think the government ought to have been much surer of what would happen in the UN before it unified its forces.
I have one other observation about the Middle East, and this concerns the activities of the Secretary General of the United Nations. He of course is the United Nations senior administrative officer, and it is his duty and job to carry out the resolutions passed by the Security Council and the General Assembly. Granted, many UN resolutions are somewhat vague and subject to certain conditions, but I feel that in this instance, before summarily dismissing the UNEF, the Secretary General ought to have consulted the Security Council. I think what he did went beyond what he has discretion to do. He may have had some colour of right for his actions, but I think he went beyond proper discretion in the use of his office.
[DOT] (8:20 p.m.)
It may be said that perhaps it would have been dangerous to call a meeting of the Security Council to discuss this issue before there had been prior consultation. The Secretary General is now in Cairo, I understand, trying to work out some agreement in connection with this matter. But I think he might well have gone to Cairo to see what he could do before he summarily dismissed the peace keeping force. Then, if his efforts proved unsuccessful, he could have referred the question to the Security Council. I have known the Secretary General for many years and I have great respect for him. Nevertheless in this case I think his judgment erred, though I hope of course that his present efforts are successful.
I turn, now, to the problem in Asia, which I call the Chinese problem because Viet Nam is only one facet of it. The Peking government has made its ultimate intentions clear on numerous occasions. It wishes to recover all the land lost to China in the last century-land taken from her by European countries, including Russia. She intends to recover this land, Taiwan, or Formosa, included, and she
May 23, 1967



also wishes to regain her sphere of influence in the surrounding territories of Asia including southeast Asia and particularly the part which is now North and South Viet Nam.
At the present time China appears to be a particularly difficult country with which to deal. We have all seen evidence of this. Diplomats representing countries which have been very anxious to recognize China have been dragged through the streets; their wives and children have been beaten up, put in fear of their lives and made to do all sorts of things which are degrading. Some years ago, rightly or wrongly, the United States decided that it was advisable to check Chinese expansion by entering South Viet Nam at the request of the South Viet Nam government. This request was made because a revolutionary group known as the Viet Cong, assisted and abetted by North Viet Nam by the infiltration of war materials, weapons and men, was making the task of the civilian government impossible. The attack was, in fact, similar to the attack made on south Korea a few years earlier. In passing, it is worthy of note that in modern days war does not necessarily mean some formal military activity; it can equally mean subversion, infiltration and so on, varieties of modern warfare which are just as effective.
Another point is worth noting, one which is often disregarded in the press and elsewhere. The United States is not the only nation which is closely concerned in this affair. Asian and Pacific nations are just as concerned. I refer to Korea, the Philippines, Australia, New Zealand, Thailand and Japan, to mention only a few. Australia, New Zealand, the Philippines and south Korea have troops actively fighting in South Viet Nam-a fact which is often overlooked or played down for some reason. The United States is not the only country which has troops there. These other countries have forces there as well.
Recently there has been a great deal of talk about the bombing of North Viet Nam. The United States has made it clear that as long as military supplies, weapons and men continue to enter South Viet Nam from North Viet Nam it will be extremely difficult for the government of South Viet Nam to control that country effectively, and that the flow of these supplies must be stopped. It has also been made clear-and some of our United States colleagues made this clear to us the other day-that the United States recognizes that if North Viet Nam were openly invaded by
Foreign Policy
United States forces there would be great danger of China actively entering the conflict.
Demands are repeatedly made that the bombing should be stopped. All of us are interested in seeing a negotiated peace. If there is a possibility that stopping the bombing in North Viet Nam would assist in bringing about these negotiations, I think we would all be in agreement. As has been suggested by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker), by the spokesman for the New Democratic party and by a great many others outside this house, stop the bombing and see what happens. Frankly, I do not see that it would make any difference. But if there is any hope of results from such a move I think it should be tried. Certainly, the bombing of Hanoi and Haiphong might well cease for a period of time to see whether the other side responds; but it must be remembered of course, that on previous occasions when bombing was stopped North Viet Nam simply profited by the occasion to deliver enormous quantities of supplies and military equipment into South Viet Nam resulting in a substantial increase of hostilities there. As an experiment it certa.nly might be worth while to cease bombing Hanoi and that area, even at the risk of this happening again, but I certainly think that the immediate supply routes from the north to the south should not be given this immunity unless some undertaking is received to stop the flow of supplies.
One interesting suggestion has been made-and I am led to understand it is presently in process of being carried out. It is that in order to stop effectively the flow of military supplies from North to South Viet Nam a wall be built across the country between the north and south, and extended through Laos. This would of course be a very expensive project. The idea, as I understand it, would be to build some sort of wall or fence which would be cleared of vegetation on both sides and which would effectively prevent infiltration. It must be extended through Laos-otherwise it would be like the old Maginot Line which was not extended across the Belgian frontier, and was not therefore very effective.
If such a wall or fence were completed in the near future it would of course greatly reduce the necessity for any bombing or active hostilities in North Viet Nam itself. It would seal off the flow of military supplies from the north and enable the government of South Viet Nam to look after its own territory without having to worry about the further

Foreign Policy
infiltration of men and war material. There is one thing that was brought very forcibly to the attention of those members of the house who were members of the U.S.-Canada parliamentary group. All members of the United States delegation seemed concerned about this. It is something that we have all heard of elsewhere, and it is something that should be noted.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
A great worry of many members of the United States congress is not so much the peace movements and the influence of the peace movements in the United States -because these, we are informed, are the concern of a relatively minute group, a very small group in the United States-but rather the increasing demand by the public of the United States to use nuclear weapons.
One member mentioned to me-and I do not care to mention his name because in my view that should not be done-that in one week 27 young men from his electoral district were killed. The parents of these young men said to him, not unreasonably "When you have the weapons to stop these people, why did my son have to die?" That is a pretty compelling argument; and the great worry of these members of congress seemed to be the increasing growth of this pressure in the United States to use nuclear weapons. This was the great concern and I think it should be the concern to all of us, and something we should consider in any views we express here or in any action that is to be taken.
Those of us in this party agree generally with the government's policy on North Viet Nam. I think we might try to send more medical help, particularly for civilians, children and the like. I also agree that we should certainly keep our position on the International Control Commission. It has not done anything yet to speak of, but it may in the future form a valuable potential springboard from which some sort of negotiations may come, and I think that is worth while. But I think our position in this regard on the International Control Commission, and our other positions on Viet Nam should be much better publicized to the general public. The people of Canada do not seem to be aware of our position in this regard and of why we are maintaining it. I am surprised at the minister in this regard, because he is usually diligent in communicating his views to the public. Over the years he has achieved a great deal of experience in this regard, and I think if he exercised some of this experience with the
[Mr. Nesbitt.!
May 23, 1967
department, in making sure the public is better informed of what our position is and why, it would be very helpful, and would subject the government to less criticism.
We have heard a great deal about getting peace negotiations started and these must eventually take place as neither side can win the present conflict in Viet Nam. The United States and others have tried repeatedly to get North Viet Nam to the conference table, but there has always been an unequivocal No. I have heard it said that the United States has had no contact with China in this regard, but I have been assured that the United States government on numerous occasions has had direct contact with the government of Peking, and each time it tried to discuss the matter, the Peking government brought up the subject of Taiwan and said that until that was settled there could be no negotiations on anything in Asia.
A great many people have said that the United States is not serious in its peace efforts, that its peace efforts are phony and the like. I do not believe this, I do not think it is true. I believe the United States, recently at least, has made repeated efforts to try to get negotiations going. SO far as I am concerned, I do not think there is any likelihood of peace negotiations at the present time or of any immediate stop to the Vietnamese war. I believe this for several reasons, the main one being that I do not think the Chinese will permit any negotiations to take place. I think Chinese interests are being served by a continuation of the war in Viet Nam.
This conflict is one of the principal items, if not the principal item, preventing further closer association between the United States and the Soviet union. In the last year at the United Nations in a number of fields, on the Security Council, in the non-proliferation treaty and elsewhere, there was an increasingly closer co-operation between the United States and the U.S.S.R. and this, of course, does not serve the present interests of the existing government in Peking. There is little doubt, because of geographical proximity and other things, that the voice of Peking in North Viet Nam must be pretty strong, and this is one of the three reasons that the Chinese government is unlikely to permit North Viet Nam to make peace at the present time.
The second reason of course is that this war is a tremendously costly war to the United States, not only in materials but in men and manpower. The more the Chinese can bleed
May 23, 1967



the United States in this war, the happier they are, and it is not costing the Chinese any manpower, despite the vast numbers they have. It is costing the lives of other people, the North Vietnamese, but it is certainly not in the interests of the Chinese to stop the cost to the United States.
My third reason for saying this is that those in this house who have had some experience of negotiating with communist countries have always found that if any communist-type country sees any likelihood whatsoever of your changing your position, even one sixteenth of an inch, they will remain absolutely adamant hoping you will change.
They do not have to answer to an electorate. In this country we think other people react like we do because we always interpret others in terms of ourselves. But in communist countries they do not have to answer to an electorate. They have one position one day, and they change it overnight-I have seen it happen-and it does not make any difference to anyone.
I think the North Vietnamese and the Chinese feel that as long as they can keep up pressure on the United States abroad, with people condemning the United States for bombing the North and the like, and keep up pressure on the United States at home through peace movements and the like, the United States government may not be forced to withdraw entirely but may be forced to moderate greatly its position in favour of the North Vietnamese. As long as they think there is the slightest likelihood of this happening, I do not see any likelihood of any serious negotiations.
[DOT] (8:40 p.m.)
The facts of life, whether one likes it or does not like it, is that, regardless of the reasons and results, the United States is in South Viet Nam and the United States simply cannot turn tail, run, and get out. Any Americans I have talked to in the last few months, regardless of their views on how the war may or may not be conducted, have been quite firm on this. The United States is not going to get out of Viet Nam. It is not going to turn tail and run, because if it did it would open up a regular Pandora's box all over the world.
The Russians and the Chinese would be encouraged to start activities in every trouble spot in Asia, South America, or anywhere else. Believe me, Mr. Speaker, the present sweetness and light that they flaunt in Europe is not because of their love of the United
Foreign Policy
States. It is because of NATO and because of the increased strength of the United States and western Europe. Russian long range objectives remain, despite the fact that at present they look quite peaceful. But anywhere they can find a soft spot which they can use, they will open it up, and if the United States turned tail and ran in Viet Nam we know exactly what would happen. If you think there is trouble now, it is nothing to what there would be then.
There are one or two other things I would like to mention in concluding. The first is the strength of the views of Canadians in the world. We are a nation that I think is well respected throughout the world, and well liked, but I think we should understand that we cannot rally world opinion, as the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) rather naively put it this afternoon.
You may try to rally all the opinion you like, but when a major power like the United States, or China, or the Soviet Union is irrevocably committed to something, it is not going to be influenced very much by what smaller countries think. All you have to do is remember what happened in Hungary. A great storm was raised throughout the world about what the Soviet union did in Hungary, but the Soviet union did not pay one iota of attention because the Russians felt their vital interests were concerned. The Americans think just as strongly about Viet Nam, and if Canada went out to rally public opinion throughout the world on this subject, I do not think it would have very much effect on the United States. You have to be realistic about this.
There is one thing I think Canada can do in this regard. It is not something we can do today or tomorrow, and perhaps not for years, because I think the present temper of the government of Peking is such that it is not now possible to deal with them. If we should send an envoy there, it is possible that he would be dragged through the streets. We cannot expect people to go there under these conditions. Undoubtedly, however, this will settle down. I believe it is quite clear that the other western nations, particularly the United States, cannot continue to have relations with a country like China, which are likely to lead to war at any time. Something must be done in an effort to normalize relations between the two countries. Because of political and other reasons I do not think it is possible for the United States to make these overtures even in the reasonably near future; nor do I

May 23, 1967
Foreign Policy
think it is likely that the Chinese would do the right hon. Leader of the Opposition asks so, because of their rather deep rooted dislike the government to tell all, tell everything for the United States. I think there is one they know, and express their inner thoughts, country which can do this, and that country is
Canada.

Oh, oh.
Already Canada has made a start. The hon. member for Qu'Appelle (Mr. Hamilton) when he was minister of agriculture got this country's toe in the door by starting to sell wheat in open trade with China. Improvement of relations will take a long time; it will not be done overnight. The Chinese are a very proud people and they certainly were dealt with badly by the western nations in the last century. We must look ahead ten, 15, 20 years, or even longer into the future. I think Canada might be the country which, above all other nations, is best able to do this. The British, the French, the Germans and others, certainly the Russians, are not in the same position because of their activities in years gone by. We have had successful trade relations with China and I think, while at the present time it probably is out of the question, that just as soon as we seen an opportunity the government should do everything it can to try to get its toe a little further in the Chinese door, with the hope that it might be able to normalize relations as soon as this conveniently can be done not only on behalf of this country but on behalf of the western world.
I see that my time is up, Mr. Speaker. All I should like to say to the minister in this connection is that I think he might save himself and his government a great deal of trouble if he could be a little more forthcoming with information on important subjects such as Viet Nam and the Middle East, and give greater publicity to the reasons for the government's activity. The Canadian people are uncertain concerning our objectives and the objectives of the United States. It is this uncertainty which causes the great unease in Canada. This uncertainty is aided and abetted by the Canadian Broadcasting Corporation and some of its friends.

Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) regrets that the government has neglected or refused to make available time to debate international problems, and regrets that the government has failed to state the policies of our country with clarity, without uncertainty, and unequivocally, with regard to Asia and the Middle East. To summarize that motion,

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
Well, I have heard that interjection and although it would take him a long time I think it would do my friend some good if he would read some of the rather scholarly speeches on Asia made by the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin). I would suggest by way of a starter that he read the series of three speeches delivered by the minister at Columbia University in the Blaustein Foundation, which lectures are being studied all over the world by students of the Far East.
The subamendment moved by the hon. member for York South (Mr. Lewis) regrets that the government has failed to do everything in its power to press the United States to stop the bombing of North Viet Nam, and so on. To summarize the subamendment, we are asked by the New Democratic party to attack or criticize the United States. So the official opposition asks the government to tell everything they know, and the New Democratic party suggests we take a good crack at the United States. It may be contended that either or both of these resolutions in effect say that the government should get off the International Control Commission and cease to use what offices it has in respect to this important dispute.
Everyone in Canada knows that the position of the Canadian forces now in the Middle East is sensitive and critical. No leader representing his country in international affairs could have been expected to do more than has been done by the Secretary of State for External Affairs even in the last few hours with regard to this very delicate situation. Certainly nobody knows better than this government how pregnant with disaster the situation in the Middle East may actually be.
What possible good would be achieved if the government were to reverse its policy of impartiality in this disturbing area where we pray, above all else, that violence will not erupt. What possible good would it do, except to make a show of ourselves as a country, if we were to attack verbally either of the parties in the far east.
Would the hon. member permit a question?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Prime Minister
speechtext:
If there are questions, I think it would be better that they be asked at the conclusion of my comments. The hon.
May 23, 1967

member for Oxford (Mr. Nesbitt), speaking a moment ago, referred to the fact that a number of countries are involved in the complex developments in Viet Nam. Recently I obtained a copy of a study by a number of responsible people with regard to the economic, political and military developments since 1960 in Laos, Thailand, Burma, Cambodia, South Korea, Japan, Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, New Zealand and Australia, all of which countries in some degree are interested very directly in a solution to the Viet Nam problem.
As the hon. member for Oxford indicated, South Korea, the Philippines, New Zealand and Australia are involved with a military commitment. I believe sincerely the quality of leadership which has come from Canada at this stage is the most hopeful there is with regard to a possible solution. May I read just a part of the evidence given by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to the House of Commons standing committee on external affairs on April 11, 1967. This was no niggardly statement. There are 18 pages of evidence; the statement is pretty exhaustive. However, the essence of it I believe is summarized pretty well at page 11 where it says:
In response to those who have asked the government to dissociate itself from the bombing of North Viet Nam by the United States, we have made it clear that we would, indeed, like to see the bombing stopped, hut that we would also like to see the infiltration stopped, and that we would like to see negotiations looking towards the peaceful solution of this conflict begun.
He went on:
[DOT]-it will continue to be the object of our diplomatic efforts to try to establish a basis on which the two sides might be brought together.
May I ask hon. members what they think could be accomplished by Canada voicing its views with regard to the merits of either side of the issue.
[DOT] (8:50 p.m.)
That, of course, means dissociation from the only body which might possibly be successful in this complex situation, namely the International Control Commission. On February 13 the Secretary of State for External Affairs urged his critics in parliament and across the country to understand the circumstances under which our foreign policy must be conducted. He said at that time that in matters of negotiation, particularly in respect of war and peace, the government should not be expected on every occasion to make disclosures which would not be in the
Foreign Policy
best interests of achieving those things everyone has in mind. This seems to be what we are coming back to, because the Leader of the Opposition suggests that we should disclose everything, tell all and give complete details about our proposals, what has been said and what we have done. The Secretary of State for External Affairs has urged the efficacy of quiet diplomacy.
It was my privilege on several occasions last summer to talk to Anthony Eden, now Lord Avon, who came to Canada to honour the Brockville Rifles on the occasion of their centennial. At that time I had the opportunity to discuss Viet Nam with this renowned diplomat, who played such a very active role in Geneva in 1954. I do not think I am inaccurate or incorrect when I say that Lord Avon had nothing but praise for the energy, knowledge and resourcefulness of Canada as it contrived to bring some sort of sanity out of the lunacy in Viet Nam.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs told us that it would be self-defeating for us as Canadians to be neutral if statements were made that had the effect of slamming doors, and it is perfectly clear that doors are still open. Many people in the world wonder why it is that we are able to carry on quiet and discreet discussions at different levels with various people in opposite camps. He referred to two missions undertaken by Chester Ronning last year in this regard, and there are many others.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs indicated that the International Control Commission might not, in the end, be the instrument that would be used to promote a settlement. Perhaps there will be a third world war which will be final. Surely we can hope that this will not be the case. It is Canada's duty to be ready and able to exploit every opportunity to achieve a settlement. The Secretary of State for External Affairs said there may be a special role for us to play in the Viet Nam situation as it is now unfolding. I should like to ask who in the house is in a better position to judge that possibility than the Secretary of State for External Affairs.
Recently when I was in Asia I picked up a number of newspapers which covered the John Steinbeck reports. He said that there was a new kind of warfare in Viet Nam with no fronts and no rear. He said "It is a feeling war."

In one of his speeches, and I have forgotten which one, the Secretary of State for External Affairs referred to the complex strands of the controversy. A wise speech was delivered in Brockville by Tom Gould, who has substantial knowledge of the country from personal observation. He referred to the complexities of the war in this land that has been divided for many, many years by the natural divisions in the hills and valleys in the north and south, as well as by differences of dialect.
The most useful material I have seen in respect of Viet Nam is contained in the second lecture delivered by the Secretary of State for External Affairs to Columbia University on April 27, 1967. As I say, this was the second in a series of three lectures. This contains some useful factual information that might well be recalled.
On that occasion speaking to an international audience he said:
The Geneva conference of 1954, which brought an end to hostilities in Viet Nam, Laos and Cambodia, was the classic case of the attempt at peaceful resolution of conflict outside the United Nations context.
In his earlier address the Secretary of State for External Affairs said, regarding the role of peacekeeper:
If, in our judgment, the peace keeping role in any particular case should not be consistent with Our conception of a just or speedy settlement or with our national interests we would not hesitate to decline or to terminate Canadian participation. If we do participate, it is because in all the circumstances we believe it to be the most appropriate and most helpful action for us to take.
The fact that Canada is committed to this job on the International Control Commission does not mean that Canadians have no feelings, knowledge, information or opinions as to the rights and wrongs of any particular dispute, be it in Kashmir, Gaza the Congo or Viet Nam. It does mean that while we take part in certain discussions by reason of international arrangement we have the good sense to play that game according to the rules, and the rules dictate that we do our job with quiet diplomacy, with all the knowledge we have and in good faith, without taking sides. As Mr. Martin said in New York:
We have taken that action each time we have been asked to do so. Our general view has been that the UN is the most suitable international instrument to keep the peace. There are many strands woven into the complex fabric of the Viet Nam tragedy.
As we all know, Canada has played many roles in the international family. It has been a loyal member of NATO. It was a member of the United Nations forces in the Korean war. It has been a participant in nearly every
May 23. 1967

peace keeping operation that has been undertaken by the United Nations. The Secretary oi State for External Affairs told the Americans and his audience at Columbia who came from every country, that the problem in Viet Nam has represented the most frustrating, the most disillusioning, the most complex and the most difficult role that Canada has ever assumed in the international field. The present division of Viet Nam is not new. There was a wall separating two warring dynasties in the 17th and 18th centuries. We cannot forget this when we look at the difficulties today. The isolation of the villages of South Viet Nam from central authority is not a modern phenomenon, but simply a continuation of a problem which even the most illustrious and powerful emperors of Viet Nam were seldom if ever able to resolve.
Recently I spoke separately to four Ottawa ladies who are married to Canadians. They were all Vietnamese and had come from different parts of Viet Nam, with different ideological and social backgrounds. I realized after talking to these interesting people, who loved Canada even after the short while they had been here, how very complex this situation really is. As I read some of the studies that have been prepared by other countries, Australia, the Philippines, South Korea, Laos and Thailand, it is clear that these Asians who are intimately involved with the dispute recognize how very complex it is.
It seems passing strange that Canadians in Ottawa, Toronto, Montreal and Winnipeg think that somehow or other by a simple process of logic they can come to easy solutions in respect of problems that have not been resolved by indigenous people at least for decades. We know that Viet Nam is a country that has been occupied by the French since world war II. When the Geneva powers met in 1954 the war in Viet Nam had been in progress for eight years and it had spilled over into Laos and Cambodia. We sometimes forget this fact. It seems to me that we concentrate too much on the present and overlook some of the frightening things that have happened in Asia in recent times.
I have been told, for instance, that in Indonesia, which I think has a population of something like 110 million people, since the coup in 1965 well over 500,000 people have been killed and over 1,200,000 injured. I am not aware of any comment or concern in Canada about this situation. I remember some time ago in London having a discussion with a brigadier from Pakistan who was annoyed
Foreign Policy
that Canadians had no concept of the hundreds of thousands of people who had starved in his country. There was no comment at all in Canada on this situation. I am not trying to minimize the deaths in Viet Nam. Every single death, every eye out, every child who loses an arm or is injured in any way is evidence of a shocking situation. Every death is infamous; and war is something that we all hate. Surely there is no element in this house that is more righteous than any other in this desire and concern for peace.
The difficulties in Viet Nam were not caused by the simple case of a war between France on the one side and all Vietnamese nationalists, led by the communists, on the other. It is much more complex than that. Nationalist non-communist elements within the Viet Minh were gradually denuded of power and influence or completely eliminated. The French at the same time found themselves allied with many Vietnamese who were just as determined as the Viet Minh to achieve an independent Viet Nam, but who were prepared to pursue their objective by political rather than military means and who were as least as opposed to communist control as to French colonialism.
Surely as a country we, although committed to the democratic way of life and passionately, I hope, committed to freedom, are prepared in our economic and international affairs to agree that the world is pluralistic; it consists of different systems, different ideological groupings, and I am sure we are not trying, nor do I believe the United States is trying to impose its political or economic structure, its system of government on other parts of the world.
I would commend to my hon. friend from York South (Mr. Lewis) the statement of Arthur Goldberg to the Foreign Correspondents Club in Tokyo, which was reported very carefully in the newspapers-this was during the late days of February of this year -at the beginning of his fact finding trip. He said very clearly to my recollection that the United States did not want to stay there, did not intend to stay in that part of the world, did not intend to occupy any country, did not intend to impose its system of government on the people; but that they, of course, were not prepared, either, to abandon their commitments to South Viet Nam under pressure of force.

The democratic republic of Viet Nam was recognized by all the countries of the communist bloc in 1954. The state of Viet Nam was recognized by more than 30 other countries. Today when we discuss the Viet Nam problem and try to do so objectively and impartially, we have to recognize how complex, as the Secretary of State for External Affairs has said, are the strands which not only complicate the matter in that peninsula but also affect neighbourhood countries.
I remember talking to Canadian boys who went to Korea. They thought they were serving the cause of peace, just as 1 think Canadians have believed to be the case in virtually every war. But if Korea had collapsed, what would have happened would have been a movement of communist forces toward the sea of Japan and the East China Sea. Of course, the situation in Viet Nam is altogether different. They have neighbours in Cambodia, Thailand and Laos, Burma is very close, and of course to the north there is China. I think it is clear that Canadians, by their posture, seek to be friends of the Chinese, the Russians and all those people whose views ideologically are far apart from our own. I think that is our posture, and I believe it is credible. I think it is the only way in which we can usefully serve at this moment of history.
We did not expect to be invited into the International Control Commission when the invitation was extended to India and Poland. We knew that Poland was the nominee of the Bandung group, and India was invited to become a member of the commission because she was ostensibly neutral. Canada could very easily have taken the position of always supporting the west. I think it is fair to say that when Canada was recommended, Communist China had envisaged a troika arrangement in which Poland would represent the interests of one of the parties, Canada would represent the interests of the other and Ind a would have, in effect, the deciding vote.
As the Canadian representatives began to examine the problem of their responsibility I think they came to the conclusion that this was imposing an intolerable burden on the one neutral member of the commission. That is to say, if Canada always took the position of the west, as a nonrnee might in a labour arbitration representing either labour or capital, and left it to the third member to have the deciding vote, this would not serve any useful purpose. So Canada decided from the

very beginning-and this point the Secretary of State for External Affairs made clear, and he pointed it out fearlessly to his American friends and to those in the other parts of the world, in Poland and in Russia-that we would try to avoid being a rigid advocate for the west. Speaking for myself I would not have much respect for a member in this House of Commons who did not have some strong views on this issue right now. All of us could blurt out

The political objectives of the governments representing the two communities of Viet Nam were in direct conflict, and this became more and more evident in the months following July, 1954.
Surely it has become even more evident since then.
One of the problems raised by Arthur Goldberg in Tokyo and elsewhere is simply the fact that negotiations which have no possible chance of constructive development are probably not worthy of beginning, although he said he was prepared to make any kind of attempt. It seems to me we have to live according to the maxim that no man is an island, that in fact we are all related one with the other, and that we are all deeply involved. I do not think we should be quitters even in the cause of peace. We would not be quitters in the cause of war, would we? If things were difficult in a war and we were an incumbent force we would not think of chickening out, but would stay right there, whether it meant a loss of a brigade, a division or a corps. Is that not so? This is no time to pull out because we happen to be there, and things are not going as we would wish. We are there, not as fighters for war but as fighters for peace. Surely what we hope for is de-escalation, to bring the fighting gradually, steadily, but inevitably to a halt and then to find a more permanent solution.

The United States has made a vast contribution to overseas aid. I think particularly of the Asian bank in the Far East, where their contribution is matched only by that of Japan. They have made a fantastic contribution to the betterment of underdeveloped peoples. If we could all start to swing our collective efforts toward the restoration of sound economic conditions among the Asian peoples this would permit a return to prosperity and peace. We believe that this peace will come only by an international presence in that sad and troubled land of Viet Nam. Our presence on the International Control Commission may be stage one in a process of even greater involvement.
For the reasons I have indicated, Mr. Speaker, I feel it would be disastrous to the cause of peace to accept the amendment and the subamendment which have been moved. Mr. Speaker, there are two matters I should like to discuss in this debate. The first is peace keeping, the second Viet Nam.
I understood, though I may have understood wrongly, that in his speech this afternoon the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) suggested that because of the withdrawal of UNEF from the Middle East, or from its position in the Middle East, the failure if not the futility of peace keeping forces generally had been demonstrated. However, I think that later in his speech he spoke of the necessity for finding some alternative. Then he went on to deal with the question which we debated at some length last session, namely the role of our unified forces, and he seemed to suggest that because we are progressing toward a unified military force, what had happened in the last week or so in the Middle East required us now to change our direction.
Of course, Mr. Speaker, it was never the case that the unified forces contemplated by Canada were to be limited to what are called United Nations peace keeping operations. This was said again and again and was just as clearly and vigorously contradicted. This is not the sole purpose of such a force, though it was one of the purposes.

I do not wish to go back and rehash the debate we had last session, even though the remarks of the Leader of the Opposition tempt one to do so. I want to seek to deal with what he said about the apparent lesson to be learned from the withdrawal of UNEF, the lesson that demonstrated the futility and failure of peace keeping forces.
Indeed, Mr. Speaker, it is true that some of the difficulties of peace keeping have been clearly underlined by what has happened. However, I remind the members of this house that the process of growth of the institution of peace keeping forces is necessarily a matter that is attended by frustration, difficulty and occasional failure. We must remember that this particular peace keeping force was established in 1956 under very special circumstances, and for us to conclude from the fact that this force has now been withdrawn at the request of the country in which it was established that it is futile for us to worry about or to pin faith in peace keeping forces in the future would be a grievous error.
It has always been recognized that the development of the United Nations peace keeping forces was experimental; that we had to learn from experience; that these forces were set up from time to time in emergency situations in an improvised manner. It is natural that in building human institutions there should be frustrations and failures.
One of the human institutions upon which we must rely for our own security within national communities is the rule of law. Yet as everyone who has studied the matter would be ready to acknowledge, not only has the rule of law never been perfect and has failed from time to time, but its development has broadened down from precedent to precedent. If those who sought to establish a rule of law within national societies had given up at the first experience or experiences of failure or difficulty, then we would never have succeeded in developing that very essential and very necessary human institution.
I do not know, and neither does anyone else in this house or in the world know, what the future holds for the development of the rule of law within the nations of the world. But we in this country, in the special position that we are in, have the opportunity, I believe, to continue to give leadership in this field. I suggest that we should not be easily pushed aside from a determination to continue to support peace keeping activities within the United Nations by whatever means we can make available.

I venture to suggest that although something may fail or does not appear to succeed today, it will nevertheless be required tomorrow, the day after tomorrow and the day after that. The world has now reached the stage where it cannot afford to allow wholesale wars to break out. It cannot allow disputes that human beings and nations are bound to have, to be settled by the old method of war.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, even though peace keeping may be experimental and frustrating, may make demands upon our imagination, may run counter to our ideas of national sovereignty and may be something that requires patience and fortitude to establish, if we are concerned about the future welfare of the world I think we must continue, despite these difficulties and frustrations, to put the whole weight of our particular influence behind the maintenance of this particular development upon which so much of the hope of the world depends.

every member of the house will have to examine his conscience and decide where he stands on tins issue.

This was the bas c reason for the United States presence in Viet Nam.
This underlying hostility to China in our view is a tragic error; from this wrong analysis flow many tragic consequences. It is true that China has experienced a revolution which, as does every revolution, has left her isolated and ideologically aggressive. But those expert in the matter do not think that China constitutes a military threat to the western world, despite the deep and legitimate grievances she may have had in the past. We believe that everything possible must be done to end China's isolation. We believe that the main criticism of the war in Viet Nam is not a criticism of intentions, or of the good wishes of the American people; we critic ze the inherent futility of what they are seeking to do there. I am indebted to the President of the Privy Council (Mr. Gordon) for giving in his speech of May 13 two excellent quotations to illustrate my point. The first is from Doctor Blake, General Secretary of the National Council of Churches in the United States-a great churchman and a great American-who said, as reported in the New York Times of April 27:
In the second place our Viet Nam policy is wrong because we cannot win. By this I do not mean we cannot obliterate Viet Nam, north and south. We have the military power to do that. But when the swamps of the Mekong delta are filled up with dead Vietnamese and when the flower of our youth lies dead with them, what victory will have been won?
Force cannot obliterate ideas.

The second quotation in the excellent speech of the President of the Privy Council is attributed to Senator McGovern who, in a speech reported in the New York Times said this:
After all the dead are counted-American and Vietnamese-and the countryside is laid waste, we will have accomplished nothing. Having sown the wind, we shall reap the whirlwind.
We have opposed the course of the American government in Viet Nam and we have said that the government of Canada must clearly do the same thing, not because of any prejudice against the United States, or became of lack of friendliness for its people, but because we believe, as was so well put by the President of the Privy Council that the present United States policy will bring disaster to us all-to the United States, Canada, and the other countries in the western world.
There is a basic difference between our viewpoint and that presented this afternoon by the hon. member for Leeds (Mr. Matheson) in his speech. He says that the present quiet diplomacy, the modest, muted way we have of not speaking clearly on this matter is the most effective way to end the disastrous situation in Viet Nam. Our basic difference is not that we do not believe in quiet diplomacy-there is of course a place for quiet diplomacy-but that we do believe that when the world is rushing to disaster quiet diplomacy is inadequate.
We believe that everybody who feels we are rushing to disaster should join in expressing that view; the cumulative weight of opinion might make itself felt in a way that would be far more effective than any so-called quiet diplomacy at this stage. Many matters between our two countries may properly be solved by quiet diplomacy. We do not wish to discount all the usual means of quietly discussing problems that concern our two countries. Those means are essential. But when the world is faced with a crisis of conscience, when we think that with all good intentions the United States is rushing to disaster in Viet Nam, to an escalation of the war that could end by wiping out the world, nothing less than saying clearly what we thing will do. We should stop the quiet diplomacy and firmly say where we believe the present course will lead.
I know that this view crosses party lines; many in the different parties agree with the line taken by the President of the Privy Council the other day. I believe that his was a cry of conscience. I share the feelings of the

If one
were to take a globe of the world tonight and encircle every trouble spot on it in red, and then turn to that portion showing Europe, Africa and Asia, it would look like a bad case of measles. One thinks immediately of Viet Nam, of China, Hong Kong, of the Near East, Nigeria, southwest Africa, Aden, the Yemen and so on, to mention just a few places.
In all these areas where disturbances are threatening world peace the two which are
Foreign Policy
most dangerous are undoubtedly the Near East and Viet Nam. I think, myself, that at the present moment the situation in the Near East involving Israel and the Arab states, particularly Syria and the U.A.R. is the most pressing and presents the most immediate danger to world peace. Whether, as we all hope, it will prove possible to prevent war developing in this area or whether, by terrible misfortune, war does break out there, I am afraid the prestige of the United Nations has been seriously damaged.
I believe that one of the things to which we should now seriously address ourselves is the search for means by which the prestige of the United Nations can be restored. One reason why the high regard in which the United Nations is held by so many people has been diminished as a result of the precipitate withdrawal of the United Nations force from the Gaza strip is that many people fail to realize that the United Nations has no military or economic power of its own, but possesses only such economic and military power as is provided by its members. Of itself, the United Nations has only moral force and moral power. To the extent that it is able to exert economic power in the form of sanctions or military power in the form of force, it must be through action taken and forces provided by its members.
The moral power of the United Nations depends on its prestige, and for this reason I believe that no matter what happens in the Middle East a severe blow has been dealt to the United Nations and it will be necessary for all countries which believe in that organization and which want to see it remain a powerful force for peace in the world to do everything in their power to rebuild that lost prestige.
I suggest that its restoration must take the form of a two-stage program. The first, the short term stage essential in order to get control of the present situation in the Middle East, is that action be taken by the Security Council or the Assembly, or the two combined, to ensure that war does not break out in the area and to prevent the Arabs or the Israelis starting a conflagration which, because of the geographical area with which we are concerned, could readily engulf the entire world. What action could be taken, or how it could best be pursued, I am not in a position to know; the minister is in a better position in this regard than I am.

I suggest that the action of the council might be effective if the powerful nations who constitute its per* manent members were to talk in very strong and plain terms to both the Arabs on the one side and the Israelis on the other. We have heard nothing from the minister since in that connection, and I think the house and Canada as a whole would be interested in knowing what has been the reaction to that suggestion.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I was informed on Saturday by the foreign minister of Israel that, for reasons he outlined, the proposal was not acceptable. I may say that when I received this response events, had of course, overtaken the suggestion which had been made to the Israel ambassador here in Ottawa prior to the actual decision of the Secretary General effecting the withdrawal of the force.

I am sorry that that suggestion which the minister made, and in which I thought there was considerable merit, is not being followed through. In spite of what has been said on this matter I personally can see no difference between the United Nations peace keeping force being on the Egyptian side of the border or on the Israeli side of the border. In fact, I always thought it was a mistake that it was not on both sides of the border from the beginning. I think it would have been much better had it straddled the border from the beginning, as it would have made any outbreak much more unlikely than was the case when it was only on one side of the border.
In that connection I might say that when I was in the Gaza strip in the last week of 1962, and was going along the line of demarcation, which was only a narrow ditch, I jumped
[Mr. Martin (Essex East) .1
across the ditch on to the Israeli side, and the United Nations people nearly went out of their minds. They shouted, "Get back right away", and when I returned said, "It's a wonder you were not shot". It always seemed to me a great mistake to have a situation in which if anybody deliberately or inadvertently went across a ditch that size, he might be shot. It would have been a much safer situation to have had the peace keeping force spread at least a mile or so on each side of the border, and I would hope that if there is a future operation of this kind this is what might be done, because it would be much safer.
These are some of the things which I think might possibly be done on a short term basis. Also on a short term basis I think the United Nations General Assembly might take some action in calling on those on either side of the dispute to use moderation and be prepared to talk in connection with the whole matter.
At the present time it seems to me that the situation in the gulf of Aqaba presents a particular danger. The U.A.R. has announced that it is going to blockade the mouth of the gulf, which it can readily command from Sharm El Sheikh without the use of ships. From that point the gulf can be commanded by artillery fire, but the Israelis have stated that they are going to continue the use of the port at the head of the gulf. This creates a hard position, one which more than any other may produce the spark to start the conflagration.
I believe it is the duty of the Security Council to put all the pressure necessary on both contestants to make sure that shots do not start to be fired at the entrance to the gulf of Aqaba.

speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext: I have just been informed that the Security Council will meet at 10.30 tomorrow morning.

So much for the short term situation. From the long term point of view of restoring and building up the prestige of the United Nations there are a considerable number of steps which may be taken. The first of these is that the United Nations should be much more active and insistent on having some of the basic causes of the conflict along the boundary cleared up. Since 1956 refugee camps have been maintained in the Gaza strip. These presently hold over a million Palestinian Arabs whose original homes were in what is now the state of Israel. They fled from there during the war, and since that
May 23, 1967

time have been supported by the United Nations in a condition just above the starvation level.
These refugees live in conditions of complete misery. I was never more saddened and discouraged than when I spent a day going through the refugee camps in the Gaza strip and saw the conditions in which these people were living, saw the rations which were given out to them and, in particular, saw the complete lack of any opportunity for them to be able to secure an education, to learn a trade, or to have any prospects or opportunities. I should qualify that by saying there was one small trade school which was training a limited number of the refugees who, after training, were being accepted in other Arab countries as trained mechanics, etc. But that was only a drop in the bucket.
That situation is not only in the Gaza strip. It exists to a greater extent in Jordan, and it also exists in Syria and the Lebanon. In my view the United Nations has been very slow to act. Really, it has been derelict in its duty in allowing this situation to drift on from year to year. It has taken no action and, so far as I know, has never really tried to get this basic situation cleared up, a situation which, as long as it exists, is going to cause trouble and the chance of war between Israel and her Arab neighbours.
As long as you have that Palestinian refugee problem, with these people living in miserable surroundings in camps along the perimeter of Israel, you are going to have the threat of war. You are going to have border raids and anything else along that line which makes for an unstable situation. Therefore I say the United Nations has been derelict in its duty. It has not attempted to cope with this problem and find a solution for it.
I think a solution for it can only be arrived at by the countries of the United Nations as a whole being prepared to take action to accept these people as immigrants, and by other Arab countries being prepared to take these people and absorb them in their general populations, something that they have not done because they wanted these people to remain there as a festering sore in order to keep alive the bad feelings between themselves and the Israelis.
The Israelis also have been responsible, to a considerable extent, because they would not allow any of these people to go back to their original homes, and would not provide money to move them to other places, even though as part of the original settlement they were 27053-331

Mrl Speaker, on May 17 I asked the Secretary of State for External Affairs, in brief, why when our policy is to refuse to sell arms to certain countries we continue to sell arms to the United States. This is a matter which has been of considerable concern to me and to the members of this group. We all know that various	professors at universities	and	othergroups	throughout Canada	have	presented
signed petitions to the Prime Minister. I have had letters from my constituents which indicate that some of these people have sent letters to the Prime Minister because of their concern about this matter.
I see on May 13 that 172 members of the teaching staff of the University of Saskatchewan forwarded a petition to the Prime Minister, in which they say:
We strongly urge you as a member of the house to support a policy which will
(1)	curtail all military shipment to participants in the Viet Nam conflict,
(2)	seek a peaceful solution to the war,
(3)	involve Canada in a program of immediate medical assistance.
This is what we have been trying to do since we discussed this very important, unfortunate and urgent question. The members of this party completely disagree with the Canadian government's quiet diplomacy policy in respect of the war in Viet Nam, and reject the reasons advanced by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs for following this policy; Briefly, the government's argument is that it should refrain from making what the
May 23, 1967

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion Secretary of State for External Affairs term "strong public declarations" on the war on the grounds that it would impair its efforts to bring the war to an end through negotiations. The argument is that Canada must maintain a neutral stance and avoid offending either of the combatant nations so that its mediation attempts will not be rebuffed.
We contend this reasoning is fallacious. The events of the past few years have disclosed that Canada, far from remaining neutral, has publicly defended American activities in Viet Nam while criticizing alleged acts of aggression by the National Liberation Front and North Viet Nam. Hansard is full of speeches to this effect by the Prime Minister and the Secretary of State for External Affairs, and Other government spokesmen.
In addition, Canada is selling to the United States every year some $300 million worth of armanents, much of which is forwarded to American troops in Viet Nam. This is the issue with which many are concerned; this is a moral issue. It is a matter of conscience. I have heard people, even over television, say that this is nothing to be concerned about. From our point of view, however, this is a moral issue.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs says that the sale of munitions to the United States is the result of a commitment made in the defence production sharing agreements of 1959 and 1963. But the fact is that Canada has signed no agreement to ship arms to the United States, and is therefore under no legal obligation to do so. The agreements simply provide for Canadian companies to bid on an equal basis with United States firms for United States government contracts, and the $300 million in arms sales annually is the result of this arrangement. Whether or not all these armaments go to Viet Nam, what this means is that it makes it possible for the United States to send a certain amount of arms to that country.
The sale of Canadian war material to the United States is therefore a flagrant violation of our government's long standing policy, adopted after world war II, of not shipping arms to combatant nations, particularly in areas where Canadians are involved in peace keeping activities. For example, Canada has refused to supply arms to Israel and the Arab states, to Pakistan and India, to Greece and Turkey, and to other areas where hostilities have broken out, such as Malysia and Angola. There is no excuse whatever for making an exception to this policy in the case of Viet
[Mr. Herridge.l

Nam, especially when Canada is a member of the International Control Commission there.
Even if Canada had remained genuinely neutral, there is no evidence whatever that its efforts to influence the combatant nations would have been successful. On the contrary, all indications point to the conclusion that the United States has been deterred from even greater escalation of the war solely by those nations and world leaders who have had the courage to speak out against American bombing, crop poisoning, and scorched earth tactics.
It has been world opinion, as voiced by such nations as France, Sweden and India, and by individuals such as U Thant and Pope Paul, and the protests against the war by peace groups in the United States and other countries, that has prevented the war in Viet Nam from expanding into a global catastrophe. Those countries which have, like Canada, acted as apologists for United States policy in Viet Nam or have remained silent have been ignored in Washington. That has been obvious in recent days. Canada's quiet diplomacy, in short, is serving to prolong the war, not shorten it. The Viet Nam war is the greatest moral issue of our time. The world's strongest military nation is systematically obliterating a small peasant country by all the means of mass destruction in its vast arsenal, short of nuclear weapons, and we are assisting by supplying those weapons. This barbaric behaviour verges on attempted genocide, and I have no hesitation in using those words. I give great credit to the work done by the federation of veterans in this regard. These men have taken part in war and they know something about it. To refuse to condemn this behaviour, as the Canadian government has done, is to condone it.
I should like to ask the parliamentary secretary how he justifies the supplying of arms to the United States under these circumstances.

subsubtopic: PUBLIC WORKS-POINTE-MICHEL, QUE.- INQUIRY AS TO WHARF CONSTRUCTION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on the orders of the day this afternoon I put a question to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) regarding the use by jet airliners of JP4 fuel. I Have the feeling that the minister did not quite understand my question, and that is the reason I put it down for tonight's late show.
I gather I drew the late late show. When 1 asked my question this afternoon the Minister of Transport seemed to think that I was suggesting that the use of JP4 fuel was somehow the cause of Saturday night's tragic accident at Uplands airport. I am sure he would realize on a moment's reflection that I was not suggesting that at all. But, as I indicated when I asked questions about JP4 fuel on

previous occasions, it does seem to me there is something to the point of view that if an aircraft is using a fuel with a low flash point, sometimes called high inflammability, the danger of fire or explosion after a crash is greater than if an airline is using a fuel with a high flash point. It is because of this belief, which seems to me quite logical and which is held by the International Transport Workers Federation and subscribed to by certain other people as well, that I think the government should make a study of the question and determine whether or not it should ban the use of JP4 fuel by jet aircraft in Canada.
Ironically enough, when I asked the question previously- I was given an answer last Thursday night on the late show to the effect that the evidence pointed the other way, and that the matter I had asked about had been looked into but there seemed to be no reason to carry out the suggestion I had made. It is a bit ironical that only two nights later this crash took place. I am not suggesting that I know the details of the accident, but even the press release which the minister put out today does refer to an explosion taking place after the crash. That is the whole point of my concern about this matter. You cannot prevent accidents or crashes by using one type of fuel rather than another, but if there is a difference in what happens after a crash takes place on the basis of whether an aircraft is using a low flash point fuel or a high flash point fuel, surely it is common sense to try to avoid an explosion or a fire after the crash, if it is possible to do so.
Let me make it as clear as I possibly can that I was not suggesting that the use of JP4 fuel was the cause of Saturday night's accident. But it does seem to me that in the light of that accident having taken place, in addition to the investigation that is being made into the crash itself, the department should re-examine-academically, if you will, but very practically now-the whole question of the use of JP4 fuel.
As I say, I do not think it is good enough to tell me that an investigation into the crash itself has been ordered. I think the statement that was made by the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources last Thursday night now has to be re-examined. That is all I am asking for, and I look the parliamentary secretary to the Minister of Transport in the eye and suggest to him that surely he cannot answer me with anything less.
